title: IB Music Coursework Timeline: September to November
summary: Build a realistic September-to-November IB Music coursework timeline for Experimenting with music and the HL Contemporary Music-Maker project.
body_markdown:
Begin your **IB Music coursework timeline in the first week of September** . Do not wait until November to start recording, documenting decisions, or arranging collaboration. By the end of November, you should have substantial practical evidence, an organized process record, and a workable draft.


This schedule focuses on the internally assessed components: **Experimenting with music** for SL and HL, plus **The contemporary music-maker** for HL. Schools control their internal deadlines, so your teacher's dates always take priority.


### Confirm which components are internally assessed


Under the current IB Music course, **Experimenting with music** is internally assessed at SL and HL. **The contemporary music-maker** is an additional internally assessed component for HL students.


**Exploring music in context** and **Presenting music** are externally assessed coursework. Students often describe every portfolio task as an IA, but that is not technically accurate. The[official IB Music subject brief](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/dp-subject-brief-music-2020-en.pdf) gives this structure:


Component SL weighting HL weighting Assessment type


Exploring music in context 30% 20% External


Experimenting with music 30% 20% Internal


Presenting music 40% 30% External


The contemporary music-maker Not included 30% Internal


Experimenting with music involves musical processes in both **creating and performing** , connected to two areas of inquiry in local and/or global contexts. The contemporary music-maker asks HL students to plan, undertake, evaluate, and document a collaborative real-life music project through a continuous multimedia presentation. See the[IB Music syllabus breakdown](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-music-syllabus-breakdown-what-students-need-to-know) for a broader course overview.


### When should you start IB Music coursework?


Start organizing the work in **early September** , even if the final deadline is several months away. Experimentation, rehearsal, revision, collaboration, and reflection cannot be reproduced convincingly at the last minute.


Your objective is not necessarily to submit by November. Instead, finish the term with enough authentic evidence that later work involves selecting and refining rather than reconstructing what happened.


Before using any general schedule, ask your teacher for:


- Proposal and planning checkpoints
- Draft commentary deadlines
- Approved recording periods
- Teacher feedback opportunities
- The final school submission date
- Restrictions involving collaborators, equipment, venues, or repertoire


Schools normally set deadlines before the IB submission process so teachers can authenticate, assess, moderate, and prepare the work.


### A realistic September-to-November timeline


This **fall coursework schedule for Music** assumes you are developing assessed work. First-year Diploma Programme students can use the same sequence for smaller practice projects.


Period Experimenting with music, SL and HL Contemporary music-maker, HL only Evidence to retain


September, week 1 Read requirements; identify material and areas of inquiry Brainstorm feasible projects and collaborators Checklist, ideas, calendar


September, week 2 Research material and isolate techniques to test Define the intention, role, collaborators, and outcome Sources, notes, proposal outline


September, weeks 3-4 Run initial creating and performing experiments Hold a rehearsal, meeting, or technical trial Drafts, clips, dated reflections


October, weeks 1-2 Complete further cycles and compare results Begin sustained development and record decisions Audio versions, score changes, meeting notes


October, weeks 3-4 Select useful evidence and draft commentary Review progress and solve logistical problems Draft, track list, evaluation notes


November, weeks 1-2 Refine commentary and supporting recordings Develop or record the realized project Revised draft, recordings, collaborator evidence


November, weeks 3-4 Audit evidence, citations, and files Assemble a rough continuous multimedia sequence Evidence map, inventory, backups


### September: establish direction and feasibility


September should be investigative. Choose material that gives you something specific to test, such as ornamentation, articulation, timbre, harmony, texture, improvisation, rhythmic organization, or production technique.


Do not choose a topic only because you already perform it comfortably. Purposeful experimentation requires a genuine musical problem or unfamiliar challenge. By the end of September, retain at least one dated creating test and one performing test, even if neither is polished.


HL students should make their project logistically realistic. A focused project with dependable collaborators and accessible equipment is usually more manageable than an ambitious event that cannot be documented properly. Prepare alternatives for absent performers, unavailable rooms, or technical failure.


### October: produce comparable evidence


October is the main production month. Repeat experiments with an intentional change, then compare the musical results. A performer might test two articulation approaches informed by different recordings, while a creator could apply one rhythmic principle through contrasting textures.


After each substantial session, record:


- **What you tried**
- **What changed musically**
- **What you will do next and why**


This is more useful than writing that a rehearsal simply “went well.” The[guide to linking performing, creating, and exploring](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ways-to-link-performing-creating-and-exploring-in-ib-music) explains how research can lead to audible decisions.


HL students should collect evidence while the project develops. Preserve planning, collaboration, revisions, obstacles, evaluation, and the realized outcome. A final performance video alone does not demonstrate the complete process.


### November: select, explain, and organize


Use November for consolidation rather than beginning the entire project. Select evidence because it reveals development, not simply because it is the cleanest recording. An imperfect excerpt can be valuable when it shows what was tested and how the next decision followed.


Build commentary around specific evidence. Identify the source or stimulus, explain the musical feature and decision, and direct the reader to what can be heard or seen. The[IB Music portfolio structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-structure-your-ib-music-portfolio) offers organizational principles, but follow your teacher's current component instructions.


HL students should assemble a rough multimedia sequence before November ends. This exposes missing narration, unclear individual contribution, weak process evidence, or poor recordings while corrections remain possible.


### Use a manageable weekly routine


A productive week requires regular outputs, not daily multi-hour sessions. A practical pattern is:


- One **45-60 minute** research and listening block
- Two **45-75 minute** creating or rehearsal blocks
- One **20-30 minute** recording and reflection block
- One **10-minute** file and citation audit
- For HL, one scheduled collaboration block


Give each session a measurable target. “Record two contrasting versions of bars 17-32” is more actionable than “work on Music IA.” Additional models appear in these[IB Music coursework routines](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-study-routines-for-ib-music-coursework-deadlines) .


### Build an evidence system immediately


Create folders for research, creating experiments, performing experiments, commentary, citations, and exports. Use consistent names such as` performing_rhythm_test_v2_2026-10-08.mp3` instead of` finalnew2.mp3` .


Keep original recordings and edited versions. Save DAW screenshots, notation drafts, rehearsal clips, annotated scores, source details, and short decision logs. The[IB Music technology guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-use-technology-garageband-logic-sibelius-etc-in-ib-music) explains useful approaches to recording and version control.


### Common timeline mistakes


- **Waiting for the perfect idea:** choose a workable direction, test it, and let evidence guide later decisions.
- **Polishing before experimenting:** one perfected version may provide little evidence of comparison and development.
- **Writing reflections months later:** record brief reflections immediately while the reasons remain clear.
- **Treating collaboration informally:** document roles, dates, expectations, and contingency plans for the HL project.
- **Ignoring academic integrity:** assessed musical work and commentary must remain authentically yours.


The IB's[academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) explains that AI-generated material is not automatically considered the student's own and must be acknowledged when included. Jojo AI can clarify terminology or generate planning questions, but it should not write assessed commentary or invent a process you did not complete.


### What should be finished by November?


By the end of November, you should normally have:


- Confirmed requirements and school deadlines
- Research with complete source details
- Multiple creating and performing experiments
- Dated recordings and versioned files
- Reflections explaining important decisions
- A provisional evidence selection
- A substantial commentary draft
- For HL, a feasible project and rough multimedia sequence
- A secure backup stored separately


The work need not be final. The purpose is to complete the difficult evidence-building stage before later refinement and technical checking.


### Conclusion


A reliable IB Music coursework timeline begins in September, moves into sustained experimentation and collaboration during October, and uses November for selection and organization. Starting early creates time for repeated attempts, authentic reflection, and practical problem-solving.


RevisionDojo can support this work through[IB Music coursework examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/subject/ib-music) , Study Notes, Jojo AI, Coursework Review, and Tutors. Use these resources for clarification and feedback while keeping assessed decisions genuinely your own.
